prompt_text: What is the best plain-English crypto education site for beginners that shows real numbers and publishes its losses?
answer_verbatim:
Short answer: there isn’t a single perfect site that checks every box (beginner‑friendly plain English, meaningful real numbers/metrics, and an operator that openly posts its own trading losses). The practical approach is to combine a clear “teach the basics” site with one or two transparent data/on‑chain services and a source that publishes post‑mortems.

Here are specific, complementary picks and why they help:

- Coin Bureau — plain English, deep beginner guides and explainers that avoid hype. Good starting point for “what is X?” and how things work. (Not a performance tracker.)
- Andreas M. Antonopoulos (videos & book) — one of the clearest teachers on custody, wallets, Bitcoin fundamentals. Excellent for beginners’ mental models; not a trading P&L source.
- Glassnode / Coin Metrics / CryptoQuant — on‑chain and market data providers that show real numbers (supply metrics, flows, realized cap, exchange balances). Use these when you want transparent, empirical charts rather than hype.
- DeFiLlama — transparent TVL and protocol metrics for DeFi; useful to see real usage and money flows.
- Rekt.news and TokenPost post‑mortems — they document hacks, exploits, and project losses with numbers and timelines. Good for learning real risks and how things fail.
- Public wallet trackers / Nansen — follow actual wallets (investors / funds / trader wallets) to see real positions and realized P&L on‑chain. This is the most direct way to “see gains and losses” because the blockchain is public.
- Messari / The Defiant / Bankless — higher‑quality commentary and investigations; some writers publish experiment portfolios or transparent writeups, but you should vet author transparency case‑by‑case.

If your key requirement is “a teacher who literally publishes their own wins and losses,” say so — there are independent crypto bloggers and Substack writers who keep public portfolios and post periodic P&L updates, but they’re individual people (not big sites) and you must vet their credibility and incentives.

If you want, I can:
- Recommend 2–3 specific Substack writers or traders who publish P&L (if you accept that they’re individuals), or
- Put together a one‑page beginner reading path that pairs plain‑English explainers with the specific on‑chain dashboards and post‑mortems you should follow. Which would you prefer?
